results.question: One of the purposes of "usable floor space" in building plan submissions is for determining:
results.responseText:
“Usable floor area” is expressly defined in the fire safety code as the aggregate floor area excluding items such as staircases, public circulation space, lift landings, lavatories, water-closets, kitchens in flats, and plant/service spaces [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions]. The same code then uses **occupancy factors based on “usable floor area in m² per person”** in Table B1 for assessing occupant capacity under the means of escape provisions [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 – Provisions of Means of Escape, Clause B4.1]. That means usable floor area is used to determine the assumed population to be evacuated in an emergency, so **D is supported** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B4.1].

By contrast, the retrieved context does **not** show “usable floor space” being used to determine the area of a refuse chamber; the refuse-storage PNAP refers to “total usable floor space” only in setting when an alternative refuse storage approach may be accepted, not as the direct basis stated here for chamber area determination [PNAP APP-35: Refuse Storage and Collection (BD), current, Appendix C, para. 1]. The context also does not show it being used to determine sanitary fitments, nor merely to describe the area within a flat exclusive of common areas [PNAP ADM-2: Centralised Processing of Building Plans (BD), current, Part 3; Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions]. The fire safety code cited is the **2011 Code (2024 Edition)**, so if there are later amendments not in the retrieved text, that should be checked.

results.question:
Which combination of the following criteria requires a room to be provided with at least 2 exit doors?

Under the Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings, a room with an occupant capacity of **31–200 persons** must have **at least 2 exit doors**; for **4–30 persons**, only **1 exit door** is required. So criterion **(2) capacity exceeds 30 persons** is a valid trigger for 2 exit doors [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 / Table B2]. The retrieved context does **not** show any rule that a room must have 2 exit doors merely because its **size exceeds 30 m²**, so criterion **(1)** is not supported by the provided text [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 2 / Clause B7.1; Table B2].

The context also indicates that where **two or more exit doors are required under Table B2**, their arrangement must satisfy travel-distance and separation rules, including the **30°** separation principle in Clauses **B11.6–B11.7**. Diagram B2 notes a **deadend travel distance** limit of **15 m** in one case and **24 m** in another, but the retrieved text does **not** provide any rule based on **direct distance exceeding 15 m**. By contrast, the question’s criterion **(4) travel distance below 18 m but exceeding 15 m** aligns with the travel-distance concept in the means-of-escape provisions, whereas criterion **(3) direct distance** is not supported by the retrieved clauses [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 / Clauses B11.6–B11.7; Section 4 / Diagram B2]. results.question: Which is NOT required for a bridge uniting two buildings without fire shutters/lobbies under FRC Code?
results.responseText:
For a bridge linking two buildings **without fire barriers/fire shutters at each end**, the Code allows it only where the bridge is **unenclosed**, meaning **both sides are provided throughout the whole length with protective barriers or parapets not higher than 1.2 m**, and it must be **constructed of non-combustible materials**. Its elements of construction must also have the **longest FRR of the storeys it links**. If the bridge is not unenclosed, it is treated as an integral part of the fire compartment it links. Evaluating the options: **B** is required because the bridge must be of **non-combustible materials**; **D** is required because an unenclosed bridge must have **protective barriers or parapets not higher than 1.2 m** on both sides throughout its length. The Code does **not** state any requirement that the bridge be **shorter than 18 m**. It also does not use the wording “at least 50% open area”; instead, it defines “unenclosed” by the 1.2 m protective barriers/parapets on both sides.
